theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: In the workplace, what does "quality" mostly mean?
options: Using the most costly materials on every job
Meeting the customer's needs and the job's specification
Finishing the job as fast as possible, whatever it looks like
Making every job look shiny, even if it is the wrong size

questions.stem: Why does poor quality cost a fabrication shop money?
options: It means the shop must buy fewer materials
It makes customers pay more for the same job
It always makes jobs finish sooner than planned
Work must be scrapped or redone, and customers may leave

questions.stem: What is a "specification" for a job?

A note of the time each worker arrived at work
A document that says exactly what the finished work must be

questions.stem: What is a "procedure" in a quality system?

A list of tools that have been lost or stolen

So that the office printer can be kept free for other jobs

questions.stem: Where would you usually find what the customer has asked for on a job?
options: On the delivery note from the steel supplier
On the job card or work order, with the drawing

Tap it on the bench so that the jaws move freely

Remove the sticker so that it does not confuse anyone

questions.stem: Which tool is best for checking that two plates are at 90° to each other?

So that faults are found early, before more work is added

questions.stem: What is a "hold point" in a job plan?

questions.stem: What is a "first-off" check?

Turning off the first machine in the morning
Checking only the last part of a batch
Checking the first part made before making the rest

questions.stem: What is "non-conforming" work?

questions.stem: You find that a bracket you welded is 5 mm too short. What should you do first?

questions.stem: Which is the right way to correct a mistake on an inspection record?

questions.stem: Who is responsible for the quality of the work you produce?
options: Only the inspector at the end of the job
Only the customer, when the job is delivered
You are, as well as everyone else on the job
Only the manager who signs the invoice

questions.stem: You are not sure how a weld should be finished. What should you do?
options: Guess, and fix it later if the customer complains

Copy the person next to you without asking

questions.stem: What is the main difference between quality control and quality assurance?
options: Quality control is done only by customers, quality assurance only by welders

Control checks the product; assurance plans to prevent faults

questions.stem: What is a quality checklist used for?
options: To list the workers who may use the canteen
To make sure every quality point is checked and recorded
To order more welding wire when it runs low
To book the welding booths for the week

questions.stem: What does "continuous improvement" mean?
options: Always looking for small ways to do the work better
Working without any breaks until the job is done
Buying new machines every year, whether needed or not
Changing the procedure every day without telling anyone

questions.stem: You think of a way to cut down spatter on a job. What is the best thing to do?
options: Keep it to yourself so that nobody copies you
Change the written procedure for everyone yourself, without asking anyone
Suggest it to your supervisor so it can be tried and checked
Only use it when the supervisor is not watching

questions.stem: In the PDCA improvement cycle, what happens at the "Check" stage?
options: The materials are ordered and paid for
The results are measured and compared with the plan
The workers are paid for the week
All the tools are cleaned and packed away for the night in the store

questions.stem: How does good housekeeping help quality in a welding shop?
options: It means that the floor never needs to be swept again after today
It makes the welds stronger even with bad technique
It lets workers skip checking their own work
Tools and materials are found easily and kept undamaged

questions.stem: Why are safety and quality closely linked?
options: Faulty work can fail in use and injure people
Safety rules only apply when the work is perfect
Quality checks are only needed after an accident
A safe workshop never needs to check its work

questions.stem: A customer complains that a gate made in the shop does not close properly. What should happen first?
options: Tell the customer the gate was fine when it left the shop
Charge the customer for a brand-new gate straight away, before looking

questions.stem: Which of these weld faults can usually be seen in a visual inspection?
options: Small cracks deep inside the weld metal
Undercut, surface porosity and uneven bead size
Lack of fusion in the middle of a thick root pass
The exact strength of the weld in a pull test

questions.stem: Two trainees measure the same part and get different results. What should be done?
options: Use the bigger of the two numbers, to be on the safe side of the size
Use the smaller number, as it is quicker
Take the average and write that down
Check the tools and method, then measure again together

questions.stem: Which details should be on a completed inspection record?
options: Job number, what was checked, results, name and date
Only the customer's phone number and address
The weather on the day and the time of lunch
The colour of the paint and the price of the steel

questions.stem: What does "right first time" mean?
options: The first person to finish gets the best mark
Only the first part of a batch needs to be correct
Doing the job correctly so it needs no rework
The supervisor is always right the first time

questions.stem: At the end of a job, what should you hand in with the finished work?
options: Only the leftover offcuts of steel
The completed job card and inspection records

essays.stem: Explain what quality means in a welding and fabrication workshop, and why it matters to the customer, the business and the worker.
essays.modelAnswer: Quality means that the work meets the customer's needs and the job's specification: the right material, the right size within tolerance, sound welds and a good finish, delivered on time. It is not about using the most costly materials, but about doing what was agreed, correctly. For the customer, quality matters because a gate, grill or frame must be safe and must last; a weak weld can fail and hurt someone. For the business, poor quality costs money through scrap, rework, wasted time, repairs under warranty and lost customers, while good work brings repeat jobs and a good name in the community. For the worker, quality work brings pride, trust from the supervisor and customers, and better chances of a job or promotion. Doing the job right first time also means less stress and less time spent fixing mistakes. Everyone on the job shares the responsibility for quality.
markingPoints: Quality means meeting the customer's needs and the specification (size, material, sound welds, finish, time)
For the customer: safety and long life of the product
For the business: poor quality brings scrap, rework, cost and lost customers; good quality brings repeat work
For the worker: pride, trust and job prospects
Right first time, and everyone shares the responsibility

essays.stem: Describe the documents that tell you the quality standard for a fabrication job, and explain how you make sure you are using the correct ones.
essays.modelAnswer: The job card or work order says what the customer wants, the quantity and the date. The drawing gives the shapes, sizes, tolerances, material and weld symbols. The specification says what the finished work must meet, such as the steel grade, weld size and finish. The welding procedure specification (WPS) gives the process, consumables, settings and joint preparation. A quality checklist or inspection sheet lists what must be checked and recorded, and the Centre's procedures say how tasks must be done. To be sure I am using the correct documents, I check that the job number matches on all of them and that the drawing has the latest revision letter or number in its title block. I make sure I am working from a controlled copy, not an old photocopy or a picture on a phone, and I hand old copies back to be removed. If two documents do not agree, or something is unclear, I stop and ask my supervisor before starting.
markingPoints: Names the job card or work order and the drawing (sizes, tolerances, material)
Names the specification, WPS and quality checklist or procedures
Checks the job number and the latest revision on each document
Uses controlled copies and returns out-of-date ones
Stops and asks the supervisor if documents disagree or are unclear

essays.stem: Describe how you would check the measuring tools you use before inspecting your work, and explain why this matters.
essays.modelAnswer: First I choose a tool that is accurate enough for the tolerance: a tape measure for long lengths, a steel rule for general sizes, a vernier or digital caliper for small sizes, a try square for angles and a fillet gauge for weld sizes. I look at the tool for damage, such as a bent rule, a kinked tape, a worn hook or a dropped square. I check that its calibration sticker or record is in date; if it is out of date, I do not use it and I report it. For a caliper, I clean the jaws, close them and check that it reads zero, and for a digital one I check the battery. I can also check a tool against a known standard, such as a gauge block or another calibrated tool. This matters because a faulty or dirty tool gives wrong readings, so good work could be rejected or faulty work could be passed and sent to the customer. After use, I clean the tools and put them back in their cases.
markingPoints: Chooses a tool accurate enough for the tolerance
Checks the tool for damage and wear
Checks the calibration is in date; does not use and reports it if not
Cleans and zeroes the tool, or checks it against a known standard
Explains that faulty tools give wrong results; cleans and stores tools after use

essays.stem: Explain how you would inspect your own work at each stage of a fabrication job: before, during and after welding.
essays.modelAnswer: Before welding, I check that I have the right drawing and material, and that the material grade and size match the drawing. I check the cut sizes and angles against the drawing, using tools that are in calibration. I check the joint preparation: bevel angle, root face, cleanliness and the fit-up gap, and that the parts are square and tacked in line. If there is a hold point, I stop and get the supervisor to check before I go on. During welding, I check that the settings match the procedure and I look at each pass, cleaning it and checking for faults such as slag, porosity or lack of fusion before the next pass. I also watch for distortion and check that the parts stay square. After welding, I check the weld size with a fillet gauge, look for surface faults such as undercut, cracks and porosity, check the overall sizes and squareness, and write the results on the inspection record.
markingPoints: Before: correct drawing and material; cut sizes checked
Before: joint preparation, fit-up, squareness and tacks checked; hold points respected
During: settings checked; each pass cleaned and inspected
During: distortion and squareness watched
After: weld size and surface faults checked, overall sizes checked, results recorded

essays.stem: Explain what you should do if you find that a piece of work does not meet the specification.
essays.modelAnswer: First I stop work on that part so that I do not add more work or cost to something that is already wrong. I mark or tag it clearly as faulty, for example with a reject or hold tag, and move it to the quarantine area so that nobody can use it by mistake. I then tell my supervisor straight away and explain what is wrong, where and how I found it. I fill in a non-conformance report (NCR) or the Centre's fault record with the job number, the part, the measured size or fault, the drawing requirement, the date and my name. I do not hide the fault, throw the part away, or try to fix it without permission. The supervisor decides whether it will be repaired, used as it is with the customer's agreement, or scrapped. I then follow that decision, record what was done, and help to find the cause so that it does not happen again.
markingPoints: Stops work on the faulty part
Tags or labels it and keeps it apart (quarantine)
Reports it to the supervisor at once
Records it on a non-conformance report with the details
Does not hide or fix it without permission; follows the decision and helps find the cause

essays.stem: Explain the difference between a correction and a corrective action, using a welding example of each.
essays.modelAnswer: A correction fixes the fault that has already happened. A corrective action finds and removes the cause of the fault so that it does not happen again. For example, a trainee finds porosity in a fillet weld on a bracket. The correction is to grind out the porous part of the weld, clean it and weld it again, then inspect it. That fixes this one bracket, but it does not stop the same thing happening on the next job. To find the cause, the group checks the possible reasons and finds that the low-hydrogen electrodes were left out of the oven overnight and took in moisture from the humid air. The corrective action is to make sure the electrodes are kept in the heated oven, to put up a sign and a check in the procedure, and to brief everyone at the next toolbox talk. Afterwards the welds are checked to make sure the porosity has stopped. Both are needed, and both should be recorded.
markingPoints: A correction fixes the fault that has happened
A corrective action removes the cause so it does not happen again
Gives a correct welding example of a correction (such as grinding out and rewelding)
Gives a correct example of finding the root cause and a corrective action
Checks the action worked and records both

essays.stem: Explain why accurate quality records are important, and describe what a good inspection record contains.
essays.modelAnswer: Quality records show what was checked, by whom, when and with what result. They prove to the customer that the work meets the specification, and they let the Centre trace a part back to its materials, welder and inspection if a problem is found later. They also help to spot faults that keep happening, so that the cause can be found. Records must be honest and accurate; a record that says a check was done when it was not is dangerous and can lead to faulty work reaching the customer. A good inspection record contains the job number and part number, the drawing number and revision, the material and its heat or batch number, the consumables used, what was checked (for example sizes, squareness and weld size), the measured results against the required sizes, a pass or fail for each, the name or signature of the person who checked, and the date. Mistakes are corrected with one line through, the new figure, and initials.
markingPoints: Records prove what was checked, by whom, when and the result
Records allow traceability and help to spot repeat faults
Records must be honest and accurate
Lists the contents: job, drawing and revision, material and batch, checks, results, pass or fail
Name or signature and date; correct way to correct a mistake

essays.stem: Describe how continuous improvement works in a workshop, and give two examples of improvements a welding trainee could suggest.
essays.modelAnswer: Continuous improvement means always looking for small ways to make the work better, safer, faster or cheaper, without lowering quality. A common way to do it is the Plan, Do, Check, Act (PDCA) cycle. First, plan: notice a problem, find its cause and plan a change. Second, do: try the change on a small scale. Third, check: measure the results and compare them with what happened before. Fourth, act: if the change worked, make it the normal way of working and update the procedure; if not, try something else. Ideas can come from anyone, and should be passed to the supervisor so they can be tested and agreed, not changed by one person alone. One example a trainee could suggest is a simple jig to hold brackets square while tacking, so every part is the same size. Another is a shadow board for tools, so that missing or damaged tools are seen at once and nobody uses the wrong gauge.
markingPoints: Explains continuous improvement as ongoing small improvements without lowering quality
Describes the PDCA stages correctly
Ideas go to the supervisor to be tested and agreed
Successful changes become the standard and the procedure is updated
Gives two sensible examples for a welding workshop

essays.stem: Explain how a worker should deal with a customer complaint about the quality of a job, in a professional way.
essays.modelAnswer: First, listen to the customer calmly and politely without arguing or blaming anyone, and let them explain the whole problem. Thank them for telling you. Ask questions so that you understand exactly what is wrong, where and when it started, for example a gate that drags on the ground or a weld that has cracked. Write down the details, the job number, the customer's name and phone number, and the date. Do not make promises you cannot keep, such as a free replacement, unless you are allowed to. Tell the customer what will happen next and when, and pass the complaint to your supervisor at once. The supervisor will arrange for the work to be inspected against the drawing and specification. If the fault was the shop's, it should be put right as agreed, and the cause found so that it does not happen again. Finally, the customer should be contacted to make sure they are satisfied, and the complaint and the action taken should be recorded.
markingPoints: Listens calmly and politely, without arguing or blaming
Asks questions and records the details
Does not make promises beyond their authority; tells the customer what will happen next
Passes it to the supervisor; the work is inspected against the specification
Fault put right and cause found; customer followed up and the complaint recorded

essays.stem: Describe how storing and handling materials and welding consumables correctly helps to keep the quality of the work high.
essays.modelAnswer: Steel should be stored off the ground, on racks, under cover and sorted by type, grade and thickness, with its markings or heat number kept visible. This stops it rusting, bending or being mixed up, so the right material is used and it can be traced. Offcuts should be marked with their grade before they go back on the rack. Low-hydrogen electrodes must be kept in a heated oven once opened, and other electrodes in a dry store, because damp flux causes porosity and cracking. Spools of MIG and flux-cored wire should be kept sealed in their packing in a dry place, so that they do not rust or take in moisture, which would cause poor feeding and porosity. Gas cylinders must be clearly labelled and chained upright, so that the right gas is used. Stock should be used in date order, oldest first. Damaged, wet or unmarked materials should be set aside and reported, not used. Careful handling also stops dents and scratches on finished work.
markingPoints: Steel stored off the ground, under cover, sorted and with markings kept, so the right material is used and traced
Electrodes stored dry or in a heated oven, to prevent porosity and cracking
Wire spools sealed and dry; gas cylinders labelled and chained
Stock used oldest first
Damaged, wet or unmarked materials set aside and reported; finished work handled with care

practical1.title: Inspect a batch of welded parts and report any non-conforming work
practical1.brief: The assessor gives the group a batch of 8 to 10 small welded parts (for example tee joints or brackets from earlier practicals), the drawing with its tolerances, and blank inspection sheets and non-conformance report forms. As a group, first check every measuring tool you will use and record the check. Then share the parts so that every member inspects at least two parts: measure the sizes, check squareness, check the weld sizes with a fillet gauge and look for surface faults. Each member writes their results on the inspection sheet and signs it. Tag any part that does not meet the drawing as faulty, put it in the quarantine box, and write a non-conformance report for it. Finally, as a group, write a short note to the assessor naming the most common fault and one corrective action. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical.
materials: A batch of 8 to 10 small welded parts, with their drawing and tolerances
Steel rule, tape measure, try square, vernier or digital caliper and fillet weld gauge
Blank inspection sheets and non-conformance report forms
Reject or hold tags, and a box marked "Quarantine"
Chalk or paint marker, pens and a clipboard
photos: The measuring tools laid out, with the tool check written down
A member measuring a part against the drawing
The fillet gauge on a weld being checked
A completed inspection sheet with each member's signature
A faulty part tagged and in the quarantine box
The group's note on the most common fault and a corrective action
checklist: Checked their measuring tools for damage, zero and calibration date before use
Measured each of their parts correctly against the drawing and its tolerances
Checked weld size and looked for surface faults correctly
Recorded results clearly and honestly on the inspection sheet, and signed and dated it
Tagged and quarantined any non-conforming part they found
Wrote or helped write a clear non-conformance report
Took part in naming the most common fault and a sensible corrective action
safety: Handle welded parts with gloves: edges and spatter can be sharp
Lift heavier parts properly, or with a partner
Keep the inspection area tidy so that nobody trips over parts or cables
Wear safety glasses if you need to brush or chip a weld to see it

practical2.title: Make a batch of brackets to a drawing, with quality checks at each stage
practical2.brief: As a group, make a batch of simple L-shaped brackets from 6 mm mild steel flat bar to the assessor's drawing and tolerances, one bracket for each member. Before you start, write a short quality checklist for the job together, with a hold point after the parts are tacked. Each member cuts, cleans and tacks their own bracket. The first bracket tacked is checked by the whole group (a first-off check) before the others go on. At the hold point, the assessor checks each tacked bracket before it is fully welded. After welding, each member inspects their own bracket and another member inspects it again, and both record the results on the checklist. Any faulty bracket is tagged and reported. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group when the brackets, the checklist and the records are finished and the area is clean.
materials: 6 mm × 50 mm mild steel flat bar, enough for one bracket per member and a spare
Hacksaw or bandsaw, angle grinder with flap disc, files
Welding machine and consumables as the Centre uses (MMAW or MIG)
Steel rule, try square, caliper and fillet weld gauge
Blank checklist sheet, reject tags, pens and chalk
photos: The group's written quality checklist, showing the hold point
Parts cut and cleaned, with a member checking a length
The first-off bracket being checked by the group
Tacked brackets at the hold point, before full welding
Each member's finished bracket, labelled with their name
A bracket being checked with the try square and fillet gauge
The completed checklist with results, names and dates
The work area cleaned and tools put away
checklist: Took part in writing the quality checklist and the hold point
Cut and prepared their parts within the drawing's tolerances
Took part in the first-off check and acted on the result
Stopped at the hold point until the assessor had checked their bracket
Wore the correct PPE for cutting, grinding and welding
Inspected their own bracket and another member's, and recorded the results honestly
Tagged and reported any fault instead of hiding it
Left the work area safe and tidy
safety: Wear safety glasses and a face shield when grinding, and gloves when handling cut steel
Weld only in a booth or behind screens; wear full welding PPE
Remove anything that can burn and keep a fire extinguisher at hand
Treat all metal as hot after cutting or welding: use tongs and mark hot work
Clamp work firmly before cutting or grinding
